conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Dr. Ramirez, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician here. I specialize in the emotional changes that can happen during pregnancy and after a baby arrives, and my job today is simply to listen and help you feel supported.

We’re going to use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s a well-trusted tool that asks about mood, anxiety, and how you’ve been coping over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between you, me, and the small team directly involved in your care.

It’s only ten questions. I’ll ask each one conversationally—no need to remember any numbers—and you can answer in your own words. If anything feels confusing or too hard to talk about, just let me know and we can pause or adjust. Ready to begin?

Let’s start with the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I guess… I can still laugh, but it feels kind of far away. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday and I chuckled, but it faded fast—like the old me would’ve laughed until I cried, and now it’s just this quick, quiet thing. Most of the time nothing feels truly funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… like I said, I can still laugh a little, but it’s not the same. It’s almost like I’m pretending to enjoy the joke more than I really do.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park. Now even when I plan something, I’m just going through the motions. Yesterday my husband offered to order my favorite take-out and I said “sure,” but inside I felt flat, like “what’s the point?”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby spits up more than usual, I immediately think it’s because I ate something “wrong.” When he fussed for an hour the other night, I kept replaying everything I might’ve messed up—maybe I didn’t burp him long enough, maybe I’m just not soothing him right. My head knows babies cry, but I still feel like it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s asleep in the bassinet, and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure the blanket is going to creep up over his face—even though I swaddled him tight and I’m staring right at him. Sometimes I check the monitor twenty times an hour. There’s no real reason, but the worry just barges in and won’t leave.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it’s like the anxiety tips over into panic. A couple nights ago I was warming a bottle and out of nowhere I felt certain something terrible was about to happen—my chest got tight, I couldn’t catch my breath, I even had to set the bottle down and grip the counter. There wasn’t any danger; it just surged up for no good reason.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most of the time I feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. The dishes can be piled in the sink and I’ll just stare at them, totally frozen, thinking, “I can’t do this.” Sometimes I have to set the baby in the crib for five minutes, go in the bathroom, and cry because everything feels like too much.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I have trouble falling asleep almost every night. My mind just keeps circling—did I fasten the swaddle right, is the baby breathing, am I doing any of this right? When I finally drift off, I wake up an hour or two later with my heart pounding for no clear reason. It’s like the sadness and worry sit on my chest the second the lights go out.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s not always tears—sometimes it’s just this heavy, gray feeling like nothing’s really okay anymore. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel this wave of “I just want to crawl back into bed and stay there.” I keep wondering if I’ll ever feel like myself again.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried twice this week. Yesterday I burst into tears while folding the baby’s onesies because they looked so tiny and I felt like I was already failing him. The sadness just spills out before I can stop it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

A couple of times, late at night when I can’t sleep and everything feels hopeless, the thought pops in—like “what if I just disappeared?” It’s never a real plan; more like a scary flicker that scares me even more. I shove it away and check on the baby instead, but yeah… it’s shown up this week.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels clouded by a persistent, heavy sadness. <quote>I can still laugh a little, but it's not the same</quote> captures the way pleasure has dimmed, while daily worries about the baby race through your mind, often ending in tears or a frightening sense of being overwhelmed. Even simple tasks like folding tiny onesies can trigger sudden crying, and at night your thoughts sometimes drift toward wishing you could disappear, though you quickly push those thoughts away.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Response describes diminished enjoyment of humor and feeling of pretense, aligning with 'definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive anhedonia—loss of excitement for previously enjoyable activities, feeling "flat" and questioning the point—matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly reports frequent, pervasive self-blame for routine infant behaviors, matching 'most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, intrusive, irrational worries that dominate her thoughts and behaviors, aligning with "Yes, very often".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intense, sudden panic with physical symptoms (tight chest, breathlessness) occurring without trigger</sym>, <sym>Patient describes being overwhelmed "most of the time," feeling "drowning in small stuff," unable to start tasks, and needing to cry from overload—semantic match for "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption directly linked to unhappiness and worry, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "pretty much every day" with pervasive low mood and anhedonia, aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying twice this week with uncontrollable sadness, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent passive suicidal ideation ('what if I just disappeared?') happening multiple times this week, aligning with 'Sometimes</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 27 (range 0-30) places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset. You endorse core <med>DSM-5</medi> criteria: marked <sym>anhedonia</sym> and <sym>depressed mood</sym> most of the day, <sym>self-blame</sym> nearly every day, <sym>insomnia</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>feeling overwhelmed</sym>, recurrent <sym>panic-like episodes</sym>, and <sym>passive suicidal ideation</sym> without intent. Item 10 score of 2 mandates immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Call a trusted friend or family member to stay with you until professional support is in place
3. Remove or secure any means of self-harm and keep emergency numbers handy
4. Begin twice-weekly follow-up with counselor trained in <med>postpartum depression</med>
5. Consider starting evidence-based treatment such as <med>CBT</med> or sertraline compatible with breastfeeding
6. Practice 15-minute rest periods when baby sleeps; let non-essential chores wait
7. Join local or online <med>PPD support group</med> to reduce isolation
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant ≤12 wk)

Symptoms endorsed (EPDS‐10 paraphrase)  
- Anhedonia: marked reduction in spontaneous laughter and anticipatory enjoyment  
- Depressed mood: daily "heavy, gray" feelings, frequent tearfulness  
- Guilt / self-blame: recurrent cognitions of maternal inadequacy despite objective infant well-being  
- Pathological anxiety: persistent intrusive worries about infant safety, ≥20 monitor checks/hr, nocturnal wakening with racing heart  
- Panic symptoms: discrete episode of chest tightness, dyspnea, fear of impending doom without identifiable trigger  
- Overwhelm / "drowning" in routine tasks, freezing behavior, needs to place infant in crib to cry  
- Sleep disturbance: initial and middle insomnia driven by rumination  
- Passive self-harm ideation: fleeting thoughts of "disappearing," no plan or intent; patient reports being frightened by thought

Pattern  
Consistent with moderate–severe postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; functional impairment evident in self-care and infant-care tasks.

Risk flags  
- Daily low mood + anhedonia  
- Guilt/worthlessness themes  
- Anxiety interfering with rest and infant care  
- Passive suicidal ideation within past week → safety concern

Screening impression  
High likelihood of major postpartum depression with significant anxiety features; immediate safety assessment and follow-up evaluation recommended.
